_about: Cross-book name authority for the whole translation shelf. Consult BEFORE romanizing anything in a new book; one rendering per referent ACROSS BOOKS unless a book records a deliberate deviation (e.g. a period-flavor style like Chungking/Peiping in a 1940s memoir) in its own glossary note. Feed every new book's decided renderings back in on completion. Entries carry every rendering observed on the shelf with the books that used it; status 'reconcile' marks a live cross-book disagreement (article-only differences excluded). Sources: the nine completed books, 2026-08.

万国公墓.note: The Shanghai cemetery for the dead of all nations (万国公墓, ‘Cemetery of All Nations’), Chinese and foreign alike, on Hongqiao Road in the western outskirts (founded 1909); Stephen is buried here (ch28–ch29).

三民主义.note: 三民主义; Sun Yat-sen's doctrine of nationalism, democracy, and the people's livelihood, made the Nationalist creed. See the note at first appearance.

三潭印月.note: A celebrated West Lake scene, an islet ringed by three small stone pagodas standing in the water.

三马路.note: 三马路; the colloquial name of Hankou Road (汉口路), the financial street of Chinese Shanghai where the securities exchange stood. See the footnote at first appearance.

上海.note: China’s largest city and the seat of the Party Central and its underground in this period.

东方饭店.note: The Shanghai hotel (东方, 'the East') where Fourth Madam stages the storytelling that opens A-Chu's origins to him; rendered by pinyin, since the source's 东方饭店 does not map cleanly onto any one attested Republican-era English hotel name.

中原.note: The Central Plains (Zhongyuan) Liberated Area, linked to Chongqing by a secret line Liu Shaowen laid (ch41).

中国民权保障同盟.note: Civil-liberties body founded in Shanghai, December 1932 (Song Qingling, Cai Yuanpei, Yang Quan). Chapter 29 (footnoted).

中央特科.note: The CCP's clandestine intelligence/security organ (established 1927-28) that Gu Shunzhang helped run under Zhou Enlai. English 'Central Special Branch' is the form used by Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Special_Branch); 'Special Services Section' and 'Central Department for Special Tasks'

九江.note: 九江; the Yangzi river-port in Jiangxi, below Mount Lu.

于右任.note: 1879–1964; Nationalist elder statesman, calligrapher, and president of the Control Yuan.

云南路.note: 云南路; a Settlement road near the racecourse; older English Yunnan Road.

交际花.note: 交际花, lit. 'a flower of society'; a fashionable woman of the demimonde who moves among wealthy men, here Xu Manli.

伍豪.note: An alias of Zhou Enlai, from his code name in the Awakening Society; the pivot of the fake ‘renunciation’ notices and their rebuttal.

兆丰公园.note: 兆丰公园; the large park in the western part of the International Settlement, known in English as Jessfield Park (today Zhongshan Park, 中山公园), with a lake and a small zoo.

先施公司.note: Sincere Co., opened on Nanjing Road, Shanghai, in 1917; one of the 'four great' pre-war department stores. Cited in ch05 as commercial camouflage for moving parcels. Attested in histories of Nanjing Road commerce.

兰心大戏院.note: A Shanghai theatre (the historical Lyceum Theatre); He Yashu says they saw a Shaoxing opera there (Chapter 25). Romanized 'Lanxin' to match the Lanxin Western Restaurant.

关东军.note: The Japanese army in the Northeast; staged the Mukden Incident of 18 September 1931. Chapter 28.

内山书店.note: Real. Uchiyama Kanzo's Hongkou bookshop (from 1917; moved 1929 to Scott Road), stocking Japanese and banned left-wing books; Lu Xun's haunt.

军统.note: The Kuomintang's Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (secret police). The name is strictly of 1938; its use for 1931 is a mild anachronism. See the note at Chapter 4.

冯玉祥.note: 1882–1948; the ‘Christian General’ and warlord, at this time an anti-Japanese figure.

冯雪峰.note: 1903–1976; poet, literary theorist and CCP cultural figure, liaison to Shanghai’s writers.

北伐.note: Real. The Nationalist-Communist military campaign (1926-28) from Guangzhou to unify China; its approach to Shanghai in 1927 is the backdrop to Cui Wentai's story.

北四川路.note: 北四川路; a main road running north from the Settlement into the Hongkou district; older English North Szechuen Road.

北平.note: The name of Beijing under the Nationalist government (1928–49); site of the Tongyi Company’s largest creditors.

十九路军.note: Real. Cantonese army that fought the Japanese at Shanghai in 1932, later sent against Communists in Fujian.

十人团.note: the 1928 ten-man Liaison Group of Dai Li lore, retrojected to 1927 by the book

华懋饭店.note: Victor Sassoon's Cathay Hotel on the Bund (今和平饭店), the most fashionable hotel of 1930 Shanghai.

南市.note: The old South City district of Shanghai, site of the Nanshi Refugee Zone.

反省院.note: A Nationalist ‘Three People’s Principles’ re-education facility to which unconvicted political prisoners could be transferred, used as a rescue channel.

史良.note: 1900–1985; lawyer, the only woman of the Seven Gentlemen; first Minister of Justice of the PRC.

吴淞口.note: 吴淞口; the mouth of the Huangpu where it meets the Yangtze estuary, the seaward gate of Shanghai; older English Woosung.

吴铁城.note: Kuomintang statesman; former Guangdong governor and later overseas department minister.

周恩来.note: 1898–1976; then the real director of the Party’s underground work in Shanghai; the author’s superior.

唐绍仪.note: 1862-1938; first premier of the Republic, assassinated in Shanghai.

四马路.note: A busy, crowded Shanghai street (present-day Fuzhou Road), rendered by its old foreign-settlement name (Chapter 26).

国民党.note: Rendered ‘Kuomintang’ throughout (not ‘Nationalist Party’); the conventional English name.

国民参政会.note: The wartime advisory body; Dong Biwu and Deng Yingchao launched there a motion against the secret imprisonment of patriots (ch21).

复兴社.note: founded spring 1932; the book has Dai Li organizing its Special Services Section in 1931

外滩.note: 外滩; the riverfront boulevard of the International Settlement (外滩公园, the park on the Bund).

外白渡桥.note: The steel bridge at the mouth of Suzhou Creek, known in the foreign settlements as the Garden Bridge.

大世界.note: The famous many-storeyed amusement palace at the edge of the French Concession (opened 1917); a dance hall behind it is the scene of ch31.

大光明电影院.note: 大光明 ('great brightness'); a famous Shanghai cinema. Here only a passing reference (the girls touting at its door).

大冶.note: County (now city) in Hubei where the author was sent on leaving Qincheng in 1975, her daughter's family being posted there with a geological team (ch40, ch42).

大美晚报.note: Real. The Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury, American-owned and foreign-registered; Chinese edition from 16 Jan 1933.

天津.note: North China treaty port; seat of the Party’s Northern Bureau.

委员长.note: For Chiang; 'Chairman' would collide with the CCP usage a reader expects.

孔祥熙.note: H. H. Kung (1881–1967); financier and premier, husband of Song Ailing.

孙传芳.note: Warlord of the five southeastern provinces.

孙科.note: 1891–1973; son of Sun Yat-sen and a president of one of the Nationalist government’s Five Yuan.

孤山.note: An islet-hill in West Lake beside which the Yu Mansion stands.

孤岛.note: The name for the foreign-concession enclave of Shanghai between the Japanese occupation of the surrounding city in 1937 and the seizure of the concessions after Pearl Harbor in December 1941, during which the concessions kept a precarious neutral status.

宋子文.note: Real. Nationalist finance minister 1928-1933; evoked (unnamed) by the hint that 'Mr. Song's' elder brother is a great personage and the bank does Ministry of Finance bond business.

宋美龄.note: 1898–2003; Madame Chiang Kai-shek, youngest of the Soong sisters.

山东.note: 山东; the northern coastal province; older English Shantung.

巡捕房.note: The police stations of the foreign concessions (Shanghai's International Settlement and French Concession). Their Chinese informers were 包打聽.

常州.note: A city in southern Jiangsu on the Shanghai–Nanjing line.

庐山.note: A mountain resort in Jiangxi where Chiang Kai-shek was staying.

廖承志.note: 1908–1983; son of Liao Zhongkai and He Xiangning, CCP leader; arrested in Shanghai in 1933 and among those the author’s circle worked to rescue.

延安.note: The Communist base in northern Shaanxi; Ronghua’s wireless link runs between Shanghai and Yan’an. (The Party’s seat only from 1937; its use in the novel’s earlier setting is a mild anachronism, as with ‘Juntong.’)

张国焘.note: An early CCP leader who, during the Long March, split with the Central Committee over the line of march; later defected to the Kuomintang (1897–1979).

张大千.note: 1899–1983; one of the most celebrated modern Chinese painters.

忠义救国军.note: A Dai Li / Juntong-affiliated irregular force active in the lower Yangtze during the war; its Hengyang-region commander Zhou Kuilong held the couple (ch21).

愚园路.note: A fashionable road in western Shanghai; the site of Yang Yubo’s mansion.

戈登路.note: International Settlement street, printed in the source in Roman letters too; today Jiangning Road (江宁路).

戴季陶.note: Real (1891-1949). KMT theorist of anti-communism ('Daiism'); reread Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles to exclude the Communists.

戴笠.note: 1897–1946, head of the Nationalists' Military Statistics Bureau (军统/Juntong), the KMT secret service; Whampoa sixth class (did not graduate). Ordered and oversaw the couple's secret arrest (ch20–21).

斧头帮.note: Shanghai assassins' gang; linked to the killing of the China Merchants director.

新华日报.note: The Communist Party’s newspaper in the Nationalist areas.

方志敏.note: 1899–1935; CCP leader of the Northeast Jiangxi soviet; his prison diary was among the papers kept in the Tongyi vault.

旗袍.note: The close-fitting Chinese woman's dress (旗袍, qipao); ‘cheongsam’ is the established English form used throughout.

日本.note: 日本; Japan, named with England as America's two rivals in the East.

暨南大学.note: Overseas-Chinese university in Shanghai where Chen Gaoyong was a professor.

曲江.note: County town in northern Guangdong (present-day Shaoguan); wartime relief hub.

曹锟.note: Real (1862-1938). President of the Republic 1923-24, deposed and placed under arrest in Feng Yuxiang's 1924 coup.

曾家岩.note: The Chongqing district where the Eighth Route Army office (the '八办') stood; site of the narrator's 1942 audience with Zhou Enlai (ch20–21).

望龙门.note: The Chongqing site of the Juntong secret detention house where the narrator was held (ch21).

李公朴.note: 1902–1946; educator, one of the Seven Gentlemen; assassinated at Kunming in 1946.

李国杰.note: Real. Grandson of Li Hongzhang; principal of the 1933 China Merchants embezzlement case, sentenced to eight years.

李宗仁.note: Guangxi Clique leader; later acting president of the Republic of China.

李鸿章.note: 李鸿章 (1823–1901); the late-Qing statesman who launched the self-strengthening state industries Wang Hefu cites as the beginning of Chinese industry.

杜月笙.note: 1888-1951. Foremost of the Shanghai Green Gang 'three tycoons'; first introduced ch06. Pinyin form standard (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Du_Yuesheng).

杨杏佛.note: Yang Quan (1893–1933); secretary-general of the China League for the Protection of Civil Rights, assassinated 1933.

杭州.note: Zhejiang provincial capital on West Lake, where the author went into hiding in 1932–33.

枫林桥.note: Landmark on the road out to Longhua.

标金.note: 标金; bar gold of standard fineness traded for future delivery on the Shanghai exchange, the other great speculative market beside the bonds.

梅花山.note: Real. Hill on Purple Mountain, Nanjing, over Sun Quan's tomb; plum-viewing ground planted from 1929. Noted ch26.

歌乐山.note: A hill west of Chongqing; site of Xu Shiying's birthday banquet (ch20).

永安公司.note: Wing On Co., opened on Nanjing Road in 1918 facing Sincere; another of the 'four great' Shanghai department stores. ch05.

法大马路.note: A street in the Shanghai French Concession, today’s Jinling East Road; the address on the counter-notice.

法币.note: The Nationalist government's legal-tender paper currency (introduced 1935 in fact; the novel uses the term loosely).

洛阳.note: The ancient capital; in the peony legend Empress Wu Zetian banishes the flower to Luoyang, whence 'the peony of Luoyang is first under heaven' (Chapter 27).

洪门.note: 洪门; the sworn-brotherhood secret society of south China. See the note at 'a Hongmen brother.'

浙江路.note: 浙江路; a Settlement road crossing Nanjing Road; older English Chekiang Road.

浦东.note: The east bank of the Huangpu; older English Pootung.

海格路.note: Real. Avenue Haig (after Field Marshal Douglas Haig); today Huashan Road (华山路).

牯岭.note: 牯岭 (also romanized Kuling); the hill-station atop Mount Lu (庐山) above Jiujiang, a summer retreat from the Yangzi heat.

特科.note: The CCP's clandestine intelligence and security service (中央特科), founded 1927 and active in Shanghai; here Yang Muci's and Lao Yu's organ. See the note at Chapter 4.

玄武湖.note: Real. Lake against the northeastern wall of Nanjing.

王新衡.note: A friend of Chiang Ching-kuo and figure in the Military Statistics Bureau.

珞珈山.note: The Wuhan University campus hill where the author met Guo Changlu.

瑞金.note: The seat of the Central Soviet in Jiangxi, capital of the Chinese Soviet Republic.

田汉.note: 1898–1968; playwright and lyricist, author of the words of the PRC national anthem.

申报.note: Shanghai's most famous daily newspaper (1872–1949); among the papers A-Chu lays out for Muci in Chapter 35.

白公馆.note: The household of the Fifth Concubine of the Bai family (白府五姨太), the concubine's sworn sister and protector; also rendered the House of Bai.

白区.note: Kuomintang-controlled territory, as opposed to the Red (soviet) areas; the author’s underground post was in the Shanghai white area.

百乐门.note: The Paramount Ballroom, a famous Shanghai dance hall; here the house to which Young Tang is packed off.

秦邦宪.note: Better known as Bo Gu (博古); one of the ‘28 Bolsheviks’ and de facto Party leader 1931–35.

老闸捕房.note: 老闸捕房; the Louza (老闸) police station of the International Settlement, the very station whose men fired the shots of 30 May 1925.

胡汉民.note: 1879–1936; a leading Kuomintang theorist and rival of Chiang Kai-shek.

胡蝶.note: 1908–1989, the film star 'Butterfly Wu,' twice voted 'Queen of the Screen'; her lost wartime 'luggage' (largely smuggled goods) and her complaint to Dai Li triggered the couple's arrest (ch20–21).

苏堤.note: 苏堤; the willow-planted dyke across the West Lake, traditionally credited to the poet Su Shi. See the note in Fan Bowen's poem.

英国.note: 英国; Britain, named with Japan as America's two rivals in the East.

蒋经国.note: Chiang Kai-shek’s son; the conventional Wade–Giles English form is used.

虹口.note: 虹口; district of Shanghai north of Suzhou Creek, part of the International Settlement, with many Japanese residents and mills; older English Hongkew.

许广平.note: 1898–1968; educator and writer, wife of Lu Xun; editor of his Complete Works.

谭延闿.note: Hunan military governor and Nationalist elder; first president of the Executive Yuan; signed the Wuhan order expelling Chiang in April 1927.

贺衷寒.note: 1900-1972; Whampoa 1st class, Blue Shirt political-warfare leader

跑马厅.note: 跑马厅 (also 跑马场); the great racecourse of the International Settlement, off Bubbling Well Road (today People’s Square and People’s Park).

钱庄.note: 钱庄; a traditional Chinese private bank or money-shop, distinct from the modern 银行. The silk men's working credit runs through these houses, and it is a native-bank manager who will not stretch a point for Chen Junyi.

长安.note: The Tang capital (modern Xi'an), standing for the far-off imperial city in the tanci aria sung in Chapters 12 and 15.

长江.note: The conventional English form, used throughout.

阎锡山.note: 阎锡山 (1883–1960), the militarist governor of Shanxi (the 'model governor'); in 1930 a leader of the anti-Chiang Northern coalition whose armies drive down the Tianjin–Pukou line in this chapter's war news.

阿英.note: Pen name of Qian Xingcun (1900–1977), writer and literary historian; ran the ‘Wind and Rain Bookroom’ hidden in the Tongyi Company.

陈友仁.note: 1878–1944; foreign minister of the Wuhan Nationalist government; conventional English form retained.

陈布雷.note: Chiang Kai-shek’s chief secretary and speechwriter; elder brother of Chen Xunshe.

陈济棠.note: 1890-1954; Guangdong warlord ("the King of the South"), led the 1936 Two Kwangs revolt against Chiang.

陈独秀.note: 1879–1942; first general secretary of the CCP, removed at the August Seventh Conference of 1927.

陈立夫.note: 1900–2001; Nationalist organization boss of the ‘CC Clique,’ firmly anti-Communist.

陈赓.note: Whampoa graduate and head of the intelligence (2nd) section of the Party’s Special Branch; later a PLA general.

霞飞路.note: A main thoroughfare of the Shanghai French Concession, today’s Central Huaihai Road.

青岛.note: Shandong port city, host of the Fifth National Bar Association congress (1933).

青木关.note: A place west of Chongqing where the released couple settled 1945 (ch21).

青红帮.note: The Green Gang (青帮) and the Hong/Red Gang (洪帮), the great secret-society brotherhoods of Republican Shanghai; Young Tang names them as A-Chu's likely enemies after the hospital bombing.

静安寺.note: The Jing'an (Bubbling Well) Temple, which gave its name to Bubbling Well Road; the district around it, where the narrator and Helen breakfast (ch29).

静安寺路.note: The concession-era English name of 静安寺路 (today Nanjing West Road, 南京西路).

顾祝同.note: 1893–1987; Kuomintang general, commander of the Third War Zone.

顾顺章.note: Head of the Party’s Special Branch whose 1931 defection to the Kuomintang gravely wrecked the Shanghai underground.

香港.note: British colony; seat of the Party’s Southern Bureau.

马寅初.note: Economist, later famous for advocating population control.

马斯南路.note: Real. Rue Massenet, after the composer Jules Massenet; today Sinan Road (思南路). The recognition-signal address.

鲁迅.note: Pen name of Zhou Shuren (1881-1936); author of The True Story of Ah Q; the central figure of essay 3.

鸡鸣寺.note: Real. Temple by the Nanjing city wall, passed on the drive.

黄包车.note: The man-pulled two-wheeled cab of Republican Shanghai.

黄浦江.note: The river through Shanghai; A-Chu’s men dump the kidnappers’ bodies in it.

黄金荣.note: Green Gang boss and the sole Chinese chief inspector of the French Concession patrol house; Chiang Kai-shek was once his disciple.

龙华.note: District in the southern outskirts of Shanghai; site of the Kuomintang Garrison Command’s prison and execution ground.

康生.note: 1898–1975. Born Zhang Zongke; “Zhao Rong” was a working alias.

胡底.note: 1905–1935. Killed on the Long March in Zhang Guotao's purge.

国家政治保卫局.note: The Chinese Soviet Republic's political-security organ (1931–1935), modeled closely on the Soviet GPU; renamed the Northwest Political Security Bureau after the Long March.

中统.note: The Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Nationalist Central Organization Department, the KMT's civilian/party secret service; grew out of the 1928 Investigation Section under Chen Lifu.

特务.note: The word this chapter anatomizes. Originally a neutral term for “special-duty” military work, it became, in the mouths of both parties, the loaded word for the enemy's spies and secret police. Rendered by sense in this translation, and kept as tewu where the author discusses it as a word.

潘汉年.note: 1906–1977. A literary man turned master of CCP intelligence and united-front work; deputy head of the Social Affairs Department, working from Hong Kong and Shanghai. Wrongly imprisoned as an “inner traitor” in 1955; rehabilitated in 1982.

周兴.note: 1905–1975. Head of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region Security Office (the “Border Security”) through the Yan’an years; later a deputy minister of public security.

徐恩曾.note: 1896–1985. Head of the Nationalist Zhongtong; a nephew-by-marriage of Chen Guofu and a member of the “CC Clique.” His memoir is quoted throughout this book.

王明.note: 1904–1974. Leader of the Moscow-trained “28 Bolsheviks” and the CCP’s representative to the Comintern; a rival to Mao whose successive “Left” and “Right” lines the author disparages.

康世昌.note: A younger Yan'an-born cadre; deputy chief and, on the recapture of Yan'an, chief of the municipal public-security bureau.

中央社会部.note: The CCP’s central intelligence and security organ from February 1939, headed by Kang Sheng; known within the Party as 中社部 (Zhongshebu). The bland name “Social Affairs” was itself a cover.

陕甘宁边区保安处.note: The Border Region government’s combined public-security and procuratorial organ, known for short as 边保 (Bianbao, the “Border Security”); the executing arm of Communist security work in Yan’an, and outwardly the government face of the Northwest Bureau’s Social Affairs Department.

邓小平.note: 1904–1997. Here a mid-ranking political officer in Yan'an; after Mao Zedong's death, China's paramount leader and the architect of its “reform and opening.”

卓琳.note: 1916–2009. Born Pu Qiongying, daughter of a wealthy Yunnan ham merchant; Deng Xiaoping's wife from 1939 to the end of his life.

罗青长.note: 1918–2014. A young Yan'an-trained intelligence officer and “living file,” aide to Zhou Enlai; later minister of the Central Investigation Department.

汪东兴.note: 1916–2015. Rose from Mao Zedong's Yan'an bodyguard to head of the Central Guard Bureau; a CCP vice-chairman in the years just after Mao's death.

许建国.note: 1903–1965. Born Du Liqing; a veteran security officer, deputy head of the Border Security and later head of the Jin-Cha-Ji Social Affairs Department. Rendered “Du Liqing” where the book uses his original name.

谭政文.note: 1910–1961. A Long March security cadre, deputy head of the Border Region Security Office; later a senior procuratorial official.

赵苍璧.note: 1916–1993. A northern-Shaanxi local cadre who rose through investigation work; minister of public security of the People's Republic from 1977 to 1983.

李启明.note: An intellectual cadre from Shanxi and son-in-law of Li Kenong; the youngest deputy head of the Border Security, later governor of Shaanxi. One of the author's interviewees.

陈龙.note: 1910–1958. From the Northeast anti-Japanese forces; Mao Zedong's guard at the Chongqing negotiations and a pioneer of Communist counter-espionage.

凌云.note: 1917–2018. A Social Affairs Department trainee; the first Minister of State Security of the People's Republic.

林彪.note: 1907–1971. A leading Communist general and later marshal; named Mao Zedong's successor, he died fleeing China after an alleged coup attempt.

江青.note: 1914–1991. A Shanghai film actress and Mao Zedong's fourth wife; a leader of the Cultural Revolution and a member of the “Gang of Four.”

聂荣臻.note: 1899–1992. Commander of the Jin-Cha-Ji base area behind Japanese lines and later a marshal of the People's Republic.

叶剑英.note: 1897–1986. A Communist general and later marshal; in charge of liaison for the Southern Bureau, and decades on a decisive figure in the arrest of the Gang of Four.

李德.note: Chinese name of Otto Braun (1900–1974), the German Comintern military adviser to the CCP and the only Westerner to make the Long March.

布鲁.note: A White-area underground veteran; reconnaissance chief of the Border Security and head of its first Qilipu training class.

王炎堂.note: Born Huang Jintang; entered the Social Affairs Department at fifteen and became an expert on the Nationalist secret services; later a deputy minister of the Central Investigation Department and one of the author's interviewees.

三青团.note: The Nationalists' youth organization, founded in 1938 and folded back into the Kuomintang in 1947.

整风.note: The Yan'an Rectification, launched in 1942: Mao Zedong's campaign of ideological remolding and cadre screening.

熊向晖.note: 1919–2005. The most celebrated of the Communists' deep-cover agents; secretary to Hu Zongnan for a decade and, later, a senior diplomat and deputy head of the Central Investigation Department.

沈安娜.note: 1915–2010. The “red stenographer” who took down the Nationalists' confidential meetings for fourteen years; her husband Hua Mingzhi was her partner in the work.

白崇禧.note: 1893–1966. Muslim general of the Guangxi clique, nicknamed “Little Zhuge” for his generalship; deputy chief of the Nationalist general staff and later defense minister.

傅作义.note: 1895–1974. Nationalist commander in North China; his 1949 surrender gave the Communists Beiping without a fight, and he served the People's Republic as water-resources minister.

卢绪章.note: 1911–1995. The Communist businessman who ran Guangda Huaxing as a Party front and money-maker; after 1949 a founder of the state foreign-trade system.

陈嘉庚.note: 1874–1961. The pre-eminent overseas-Chinese leader of the South Seas, a Singapore rubber magnate and philanthropist; his 1940 visit to Yan'an turned him toward the Communists. Rendered in the Hokkien form by which he is universally known in English.

王世英.note: 1905–1968. A Special Branch veteran who ran Communist intelligence and united-front work in the North; later a provincial governor, he died persecuted in the Cultural Revolution.

吴德峰.note: 1896–1976. A founder of the Party's courier and intelligence systems; ran the hidden Xi'an intelligence station under a family cover and later held senior legal posts.

宣侠父.note: 1899–1938. A Whampoa first-class graduate and secret Communist working the Xi'an united front; his 1938 assassination on Chiang Kai-shek's order is the subject of section 6.

蒋鼎文.note: 1895–1974. A senior Whampoa-clique general and head of the Xi'an field headquarters; he carried out Chiang Kai-shek's order to kill Xuan Xiafu.

卫立煌.note: 1897–1960. Nationalist First War Zone commander; won over enough to give the Eighth Route Army ammunition, he was later suspected of Communist sympathies and eventually returned to the mainland.

邓宝珊.note: 1894–1968. Nationalist general holding Yulin north of the Border Region; a friend of the Communists from Yan'an, he helped negotiate the peaceful surrender of Beiping.

赵寿山.note: 1894–1965. Commander of the Northwestern Army's 38th Army, secretly guided by Mao Zedong; he defected to the Communists and became governor of Qinghai and then Shaanxi.

高崇民.note: 1891–1971. A leading Northeastern patriot who founded the Northeast Salvation Association; a bridge between the Communists and the Northeastern and Northwestern armies before the Xi'an Incident.

广大华行.note: A Shanghai pharmaceutical trading firm founded in 1932 and run from 1937 as a secret Communist enterprise, funding and covering the Party's intelligence work in Nationalist territory.

华润公司.note: Founded in Hong Kong in 1948–49 out of the Party's trading firms; today one of China's largest state-owned conglomerates.

八办.note: Short for 八路军办事处. The open liaison offices the Communists were allowed to maintain in Nationalist cities during the wartime alliance; rendered “the Eighth Route office(s)” or, where the author uses the bare abbreviation, “the offices.”

皖南事变.note: The January 1941 Nationalist attack on the New Fourth Army headquarters in southern Anhui (literally “the Southern Anhui Incident”), which shattered the united front.

韩练成.note: 1908–1984. A Nationalist general who secretly served the Communists from within; later a PLA lieutenant general.

阎又文.note: 1914–1962. A deep-cover Communist at Fu Zuoyi's side who helped bring about the surrender of Beiping; his identity was kept secret until 1992, long after his death.

双重政权.note: The wartime coexistence of a Nationalist-appointed and a Communist-appointed government in the same Border Region county; the “nails” of the chapter title.

磨擦.note: The standard term, on both sides, for Nationalist–Communist armed clashes 1939–1943; fan moca is “the struggle against friction.”

宝葫芦.note: The popular name for the Guanzhong sub-district, a Communist salient thrust toward Xi’an; Hu Zongnan called the same ground the “pouch” (nangxing didai).

肤施县.note: The Nationalist name for the county containing Yan’an; its Nationalist “Fushi County Government” ran in parallel with the Communist “Yan’an County Government.”

锄奸委员会.note: A mass body extending chujian (“rooting out traitors”) into a village-level surveillance network.

陈泊.note: Real name of Bu Lu, the “Red Sherlock Holmes.”

阎宝航.note: 1895–1968. A Northeastern Christian educator and aide to Zhang Xueliang who became a secret Communist inside the Nationalist elite; his 1941 report of the date of the German invasion of the USSR is the intelligence coup of this chapter. Died in prison during the Cultural Revolution; posthumously decorated by Russia in 1995.

关露.note: 1907–1982. Born Hu Shoumei; a celebrated poet and left-wing writer sent by Pan Hannian to work inside the Wang Jingwei and Japanese secret services, at the cost of a lasting public reputation as a “collaborator.” Imprisoned in the Pan Hannian case; rehabilitated shortly before her suicide.

李士群.note: 1905–1943. A former Communist who passed through the Nationalist and then the Japanese and Wang Jingwei secret services, becoming the dreaded chief of No. 76. Poisoned by the Japanese in 1943.

丁默村.note: 1901–1947. Former Nationalist Zhongtong man who became director of the Wang Jingwei “Secret Service General Headquarters” at No. 76; executed as a collaborator after the war.

岩井英一.note: 1899–1980. Japanese deputy consul-general in Shanghai and head of a foreign-ministry intelligence organ, the “Iwai Kōkan.” Pan Hannian ran a channel into his operation.

袁殊.note: 1911–1987. A left-wing writer and one of the war’s most tangled multiple agents—at once a Communist, a Nationalist Zhongtong man, and on the payroll of Japanese intelligence. Imprisoned in the Pan Hannian case.

张唯一.note: 1892–1955. A veteran of the Central Special Branch known in Pan Hannian’s Hong Kong circle as “the Old Master” (lao taiye); ran the inner office of the South China Intelligence Bureau.

陈焕章.note: Also known as Chen Tao. A Communist agent who, at Chen Geng’s direction, penetrated the puppet forces at Linfen and rose to hold, at once, major-general’s commissions from the Japanese-backed puppet army, from Juntong, and from Yan Xishan’s forces.

佐尔格.note: Richard Sorge (1895–1944), the Soviet military-intelligence master spy who worked first in Shanghai and then in Tokyo, where he reported on Japanese and German intentions. Arrested by the Japanese in 1941 and hanged in 1944.

中央情报部.note: Established September 1941 as the unified strategic-intelligence organ of the Party Center and the Military Commission, known within the Party as 中情部 (Zhongqingbu); one body with the Social Affairs Department under two signboards, run in practice by Li Kenong.

中央调查研究局.note: The high-standing intelligence-and-research bureau Mao Zedong set up in 1941 and headed himself; its remit, “investigation and study” (diaocha yanjiu), was Mao’s own doctrine of intelligence analysis.

梅机关.note: The “Plum Agency” (Japanese Ume Kikan), the Japanese army’s special-service organ in Shanghai that engineered Wang Jingwei’s defection, under Lieutenant-General Kagesa Sadaaki.

76号.note: The Wang Jingwei regime’s “Secret Service General Headquarters” at No. 76 Jessfield Road in Shanghai, notorious for torture; run by Ding Mocun and Li Shiqun.

岩井公馆.note: The “Iwai Mansion” (Japanese Iwai Kōkan), the Japanese foreign-ministry intelligence organ Iwai Eiichi ran in Shanghai.

特高课.note: The Special Higher Police (Japanese Tokkō), Japan’s political and thought police, which ran surveillance on suspected subversives at home and in occupied territory.

打狗队.note: A nickname for the Central Special Branch’s action squad (the “Red Squad”), which punished defectors and enemy agents; several later secret-service figures, Li Shiqun among them, had passed through it.

国防线.note: The Japanese-imposed frontier along the Great Wall between occupied North China and “Manchukuo,” which a traveler could cross only with a passport, sealing the Northeast off from the resistance inside the Wall.

满洲国.note: The puppet state Japan set up in the Northeast in 1932 under the last Qing emperor, Puyi; directed from emperor to premier by Japanese advisers.

华南情报局.note: The Communist intelligence bureau Pan Hannian ran from Hong Kong, coordinating the various networks of the region.

川岛芳子.note: 1907–1948. Born Aisin Gioro Xianyu, a Qing princess raised in Japan who became a Japanese agent and cavalry commander in Manchuria; executed by the Nationalists as a collaborator in 1948. Her younger brother Xiandong was a member of the Communist Northeast intelligence group.

影佐祯昭.note: 1893–1948. The Japanese army officer who ran the Ume Kikan, engineered Wang Jingwei’s defection, and served as the supreme military adviser of the Wang Jingwei regime.

王超北.note: A Shaanxi native who built the Communists’ second, deep-buried Xi’an radio net—later the “Xi’an Intelligence Office”—which survived the breaking of Wang Shijian’s network in the civil war.

中西功.note: 1910–1973. A Japanese Communist and China expert who worked for the South Manchuria Railway’s research arm while spying for the CCP under Pan Hannian’s system; obtained strategic intelligence on Japan’s southern advance. Arrested by the Tokkō, tried, and freed at the war’s end; later a Japanese Communist Party member of the Diet.

尾崎秀实.note: 1901–1944. Asahi Shimbun journalist, China expert, and adviser to Prime Minister Konoe, and the key Japanese member of the Sorge ring; arrested in 1941 and hanged with Sorge in 1944. Not to be confused with Ozaki Shōtarō.

尾崎庄太郎.note: A left-leaning graduate of the East Asia Common Culture Academy and member of Nakanishi Kō’s network; a different man from the Sorge-ring spy Ozaki Hotsumi.

王学文.note: 1895–1985. A Japan-trained Marxist economist and secret Communist who taught at the Japanese academy in Shanghai and later directed the Eighth Route Army’s enemy-army work and the Japanese Workers’ and Peasants’ School at Yan’an.

郑文道.note: 1914–1942. Nakanishi Kō’s Chinese liaison; arrested by the Japanese gendarmerie in 1942, he took his own life to protect the network.

西里龙夫.note: A Japanese journalist and Common Culture Academy man who joined the Communist intelligence network in Nanjing; tried with Nakanishi Kō and freed in 1945.

今井武夫.note: 1898–1982. A Japanese army officer who ran Operation Kiri, the secret 1940 peace channel to Chongqing, and later negotiated the Japanese surrender in China.

东条英机.note: 1884–1948. The Japanese army general who became prime minister in October 1941 and led Japan into the Pacific War; executed as a war criminal in 1948.

吴成方.note: A Communist intelligence officer under Pan Hannian who ran the Japanese cell in Shanghai; imprisoned in the Pan Hannian case and rehabilitated in 1982.

汪锦元.note: A secret Communist planted as a secretary at Wang Jingwei’s side, feeding the regime’s top secrets to the Pan Hannian network.

川合贞吉.note: A Japanese member of the Sorge ring, introduced to Sorge by Agnes Smedley.

池步洲.note: 1908–2003. A Japan-trained Nationalist cryptanalyst who broke Japanese diplomatic ciphers; Chinese accounts credit him with forecasting a Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, a claim not independently corroborated abroad.

荒尾精.note: 1859–1896. A Japanese army officer and pioneer of Japanese intelligence work in China, who opened the Hankou branch of the Rakuzendō pharmacy as a cover.

根津一.note: 1860–1927. A Japanese army officer and educator who founded and long directed the East Asia Common Culture Academy in Shanghai.

高崇武.note: So printed in the source; the man is the documented Gao Zongwu (高宗武), who with Tao Xisheng exposed the draft Japan–Wang Jingwei treaty in the January 1940 “Gao-Tao incident.”

宋子良.note: The name the “Nationalist” negotiator used in Operation Kiri. Song Ziliang was a real member of the Soong family (a brother of T.V. Soong and Soong Mei-ling), but the man at the negotiating table was an impostor, an agent of Dai Li’s Juntong.

满铁.note: The South Manchuria Railway Company, a vast Japanese “state-policy company” that ran the railways and much of the economy of the Northeast and doubled as a huge intelligence organ; its Research Department was a magnet for spies. Abbreviated 满铁 (Mantetsu).

东亚同文书院.note: The Tōa Dōbun Shoin, a Japanese academy in Shanghai (founded 1901) that trained Japanese “China hands” and doubled as a nursery of intelligence officers; a Communist Party branch also grew up inside it.

东亚同文会.note: The Tōa Dōbunkai, the semi-official Japanese society that founded and oversaw the academy.

太平洋调查会.note: The IPR, an American-founded international academic body that met by turns around the Pacific rim, and whose views could sway the relevant governments.

兴亚院.note: The Asia Development Board, a Japanese cabinet organ set up in 1938 to run affairs in occupied China, with a special-service department that drew the secret services under one hand.

关特演.note: The Kantokuen (関特演), a huge July 1941 mobilization of the Kwantung Army against the Soviet Union after the German invasion; never carried out, as Japan chose the southern advance.

桐工作.note: The Kiri Kōsaku (桒工作), Japan’s most secret 1940 “peace” channel to Chongqing, run by Imai Takeo; 桒 is the paulownia (kiri).

拉穆塞小组.note: Sorge’s Tokyo intelligence cell, from his radio code name “Ramsay”; the source also transliterates it 拉姓扎.

李得森.note: A Chinese member of Nakanishi Kō’s Nanjing network, arrested by the Japanese in 1942.

钱明.note: Real name Jing Ruonan; a Chinese liaison of the Nakanishi Kō cell and Zheng Wendao’s schoolmate.

刘钊.note: Pan Hannian’s secret courier in the Jiangnan area and Zheng Wendao’s Party sponsor.

张明达.note: A courier of the Nakanishi Kō cell who escaped the 1942 arrests; later wrote about the network under the name Fang Zhida (方知达).

锄奸.note: Literally “to hoe out the traitors.” The wartime CCP name for counter-espionage and anti-collaborator work; the army security departments were renamed Anti-Traitor Departments (锂奶部).

锄奸部.note: The renamed Eighth Route Army security department; kept parallel to the Anti-Traitor Committee (锂奶委员会).

边保.note: Short form of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region Security Office (陕甘宁边区保安处); the region’s counter-espionage and public-security organ.

山东纵队.note: The Eighth Route Army’s Shandong Column, the main CCP field force in Shandong.

军委二局.note: The Central Military Commission’s Second Bureau, the CCP’s radio-interception and cipher-breaking service.

牺盟会.note: The Sacrifice League for National Salvation (牧牙救国同盟会), an anti-Japanese mass body formed under Yan Xishan in Shanxi in 1936 and heavily penetrated by the Communists.

中美合作所.note: The Sino-American Cooperative Organization, a 1943 joint U.S. Navy–Nationalist (Dai Li) intelligence and training body at Chongqing; its Geleshan compound is bound up with the Baigongguan and Zhazidong prisons where many Communists were held and killed.

智异.note: Zhao Cangbi’s coined term for the point-against-point contest of stratagems in covert struggle.

杨奇清.note: 1911–1978. Veteran CCP security officer and counter-espionage specialist; anti-traitor chief at the Eighth Route Army’s forward headquarters, later a vice-minister of public security.

水原清.note: The Japanese reading of 水原清 is reconstructed; the man was a Japanese special agent posing as a “good devil” at Da’anzhuang.

何庆宇.note: Enemy-work section chief of the Eighth Route Army’s Shandong Column.

张露萍.note: 1921–1945. CCP agent who led the underground branch inside Juntong’s Chongqing radio headquarters; executed by the Nationalists in 1945.

张蔚林.note: Juntong radio officer turned secret Communist; member of Zhang Luping’s branch, executed 1945.

冯传庆.note: Juntong main-station radio officer turned secret Communist; member of Zhang Luping’s branch, executed 1945.

李茂堂.note: 1904–1969. A lapsed early Communist who rose to head Zhongtong’s Shaanxi station-room and secretly returned to the CCP’s service.

秦平.note: Border Security field officer in Guanzhong and at the mail-inspection station.

赵去非.note: Border Security field-team head at Luochuan; later deputy governor of Heilongjiang and head of its public-security department.

任远.note: Jidong intelligence station chief captured and later escaped from the Japanese.

单不移.note: Zhongtong boss at Luochuan (the surname 单 is read Shàn).

沈之岳.note: 1913–1994. Nationalist agent who infiltrated Yan’an; after 1949 rose to head Taiwan’s Investigation Bureau.

许继慎.note: 1901–1931. Whampoa graduate and Red Army commander in the E-Yu-Wan base, executed in an internal purge after a Nationalist frame-up; later rehabilitated as a martyr.

马汉三.note: 1903–1948. Senior Juntong officer; later executed by the Nationalists over the missing “Nine-Dragon Sword.”

李鼎铭.note: 1881–1947. Non-party gentry-assemblyman of the Border Region who proposed “crack troops and simple administration.”

马锡武.note: The book prints 马锡武; the documented judge is 马锡五 (1899–1962), same romanization, whose plain, investigative “Ma Xiwu adjudication method” became a CCP model.

左权.note: 1905–1942. Deputy chief of staff of the Eighth Route Army, killed at Shiziling; the highest-ranking Communist commander to die in the war.

溥仪.note: 1906–1967. The last Qing emperor, installed by Japan as ruler of Manchukuo.

王克敏.note: 1873–1945. Head of the Japanese-sponsored Provisional Government in North China.

李自成.note: 1606–1645. The northern-Shaanxi peasant rebel who overthrew the Ming.

师哲.note: 1905–1998. Security-office bureau chief; later Mao Zedong’s Russian-language interpreter.

谷正鼎.note: 1903–1974. CC-Clique figure, chief of the Nationalist Shaanxi provincial party headquarters.

朱家骅.note: 1893–1963. Nationalist organization minister, rival of the CC Clique.

陈果夫.note: 1892–1951. Elder of the CC Clique with his brother Chen Lifu.

程一鸣.note: 1909–1998. Former Communist who headed Juntong’s Northwest District; long a deep CCP source.

死间.note: Literally “dead agent”; one of the five kinds of spy in Sun Tzu’s Art of War, and Juntong’s term for agents planted to burrow into the Communist base areas.

海底.note: Juntong jargon (literally “sea bottom”) for the secret personal dossier each agent memorized—names, addresses, contacts, cipher, and oath—left on file at the training class.

汉中特训班.note: Juntong’s special training class near Hanzhong, run under the cover name “Tianshui Field Headquarters Guerrilla Cadre Training Class”; called the “Hanzhong class” (汉训班) for short.

汉训班.note: Short form of the Hanzhong training class.

戴案.note: The Border Security’s name for the Hanzhong-class case, after Dai Li, whose Juntong system ran the agents.

西北特别侦察站.note: Juntong’s Xi’an-based station (西北特侦站 for short) directing the penetration of the Northwest base areas; headed by Cheng Muyi.

吴南山.note: The Qingyang schoolteacher who graduated the Hanzhong class, came forward to the Communists, and became the Border Security’s long-hidden field operative in Longdong; the case began with him.

程慕颐.note: Chief of Juntong’s Northwest Special Reconnaissance Station and deputy director of the Hanzhong class (cover name Cheng Yi); fled to Taiwan.

程益.note: Cover name of Cheng Muyi as director of the Hanzhong class.

祁三益.note: Hanzhong-class demolition instructor sent to Yan’an as group liaison; turned by the Border Security and central to cracking the case.

李春茂.note: Hanzhong-class liaison (aliases Li Changsheng, Li Jun); turned and taken into the Border Security.

赵秀.note: Chief liaison for the Northwest Station’s Yan’an group; briefly turned, later fled back to Xi’an.

王星文.note: Hanzhong agent (alias Wang Jiwu) at the Lu Xun Academy of Arts; turned by the Border Security.

胡士渊.note: Leader of the independent cell (aliases Hu Siyuan, Hu Yaonan, Hu Youlian) planted in the Military Commission’s Second Bureau.

马文瑞.note: 1912–2004. Longdong prefectural party secretary who took Wu Nanshan in; himself once wrongly arrested in the northern-Shaanxi purge. Later a vice-chairman of the CPPCC National Committee.

李甫山.note: Longdong security-section chief who ran Wu Nanshan; later head of the Border Security office in Yan’an.

赵苍壁.note: 1916–1993. Border Security plainclothes-squad head sent to Longdong; later Minister of Public Security.

王珺.note: Social Affairs Department officer of the “Old Third Class” who traced the Second Bureau cell; later deputy minister of State Security.

欧阳毅.note: 1910–2005. Head of the General Political Department’s Anti-Traitor Department, which handled the army-system agents; later a PLA lieutenant general.

钱益民.note: Investigation expert of the General Political Department’s Anti-Traitor Department, one of Yan’an’s “three great investigation experts.”

抢救运动.note: The coercive spy-hunt of 1943 into which the Yan’an Rectification’s cadre-screening phase escalated; the euphemism “rescue” cast the purge as saving misled youths from espionage.

审干.note: Short for 审查干部, the vetting of cadres’ political histories; the phase of the Rectification that shaded into the Rescue Campaign.

逼供信.note: Mao’s three-word name for the purge method: coerce a confession, let the confession run wild, and believe it. First glossed at Chapter 1.

甄别.note: The corrective phase from late 1943 in which the campaign’s cases were re-examined and most detainees cleared.

南委.note: The Communists’ Southern Work Committee, under the Southern Bureau, responsible for the underground in the southeast and south; wrecked by Zhongtong in 1942.

红旗党.note: The fabricated charge that an underground CCP organization was a Nationalist front “flying the red flag to oppose the red flag.”

山东肃托.note: The anti-Trotskyist purge that swept the Shandong base area from 1939, of which the Huxi killings were the worst.

特务如麻.note: Kang Sheng’s image for the campaign’s hysteria: agents supposedly so numerous they were “thick as hemp.”

老号.note: The Border Security detainees held before the “Dai case” broke, mostly men merely suspected of being agents.

阳谋.note: Lit. “open/overt scheme,” coined as the mirror of 阴谋 yinmou “plot, conspiracy”: a design pursued in the open rather than in secret. Here it names the postwar contest in which each side maneuvered openly (the Chongqing talks) while racing for military position.

重庆谈判.note: The peace talks of 28 August–10 October 1945, to which Mao Zedong flew in person; they produced the Double-Tenth Agreement.

双十协定.note: The “Summary of Conversations” signed 10 October 1945 (the Double Tenth, the ROC national day) at the close of the Chongqing negotiations; its terms were soon overtaken by civil war.

冷藏间谍.note: An agent planted deep in the enemy camp and kept dormant, doing no active work, until a decisive moment; the book uses it interchangeably with 战略间谋 “strategic spy.”

战略间谍.note: A long-buried agent held in reserve for a strategic turning-point; see 冷藏间谋 “cold-storage spy.”

后三杰.note: Xiong Xianghui, Chen Zhongjing, and Shen Jian, the trio that penetrated Hu Zongnan’s headquarters; named in deliberate parallel to the “Three Heroes of Longtan” of the early 1930s (see ch. 1).

民主联军.note: The “democratic” label taken by units that defected to, or fought alongside, the Communists in 1945–46, before the CCP called the fighting a “war of liberation.”

延安大撤退.note: The CCP’s evacuation of its capital, Yan’an, before Hu Zongnan’s attack in March 1947.

跑反.note: A north-Shaanxi term for a whole population’s flight ahead of an oncoming army.

高树勋运动.note: Mao’s slogan-campaign, named for Gao Shuxun’s October 1945 defection, urging Nationalist troops to revolt rather than fight the civil war.

还乡团.note: Landlord-led militias that returned with the Nationalist advance to retake land and take revenge on those who had carried out CCP land reform.

冈村宁次.note: Commander-in-chief of the Japanese China Expeditionary Army, who surrendered at Nanjing on 9 September 1945.

龙云.note: The semi-autonomous governor of Yunnan, forced out by Chiang in October 1945.

卢汉.note: Yunnan-army general who took the Japanese surrender in Hanoi and later governed Yunnan; he declared for the Communists in 1949.

高树勋.note: Former Northwest Army general who defected with the New 8th Army at Handan on 30 October 1945.

大策反.note: The chapter title. Cefan means to turn an enemy soldier or unit to one's own side; da cefan, the "great turning," is the mass defection of Nationalist forces in 1948–49, which the author treats as the highest art of the secret war.

策反.note: Inducing an enemy officer, unit, or garrison to defect. Rendered "turning" (and "turning work") throughout, distinct from ordinary united-front persuasion.

华北五烈士.note: Also called the Beiping Five Martyrs: Xie Shiyan, Ding Xing, Zhu Jianguo, Zhao Liangzhang, and Shi Chun, Communist agents inside the Nationalist Eleventh War Zone, arrested in 1947 and executed in 1948.

不战而屈人之兵.note: Sun Tzu's dictum; the received translation is used.

电子对抗.note: The author's term for the 1947 radio contest: interception, direction-finding, and radio-silence deception. Rendered "electronic warfare" though the technology of the day was radio, not electronics in the later sense.

保密局.note: The Ministry of National Defense's Bureau of Confidential Investigation, the reorganized successor to Juntong after Dai Li's death in 1946, under Mao Renfeng.

联络部.note: The Communist army organ for turning enemy troops, successively named the Destruction Department, Enemy Work Department, Nationalist-Army Work Department, and Liaison Department.

王石坚.note: Chief of a large Communist intelligence network spanning the Northwest, North China, and the Northeast; his arrest in 1947, after a subordinate's betrayal, rolled up the whole system.

吴石.note: 1894–1950. Nationalist lieutenant general and deputy chief of the general staff; the highest-placed Communist agent in Taiwan, executed in Taipei in 1950.

陈明仁.note: 1903–1974. Nationalist general who beat back Lin Biao at Siping in 1947, then led his Central Army troops over to the Communists in Hunan in 1949 and became a PLA general.

郭汝瑰.note: 1907–1997. Operations chief in the Nationalist Ministry of National Defense and a long-hidden Communist agent who fed the Communists top operational plans.

曾泽生.note: 1902–1973. Yunnan-army general who led the 60th Army in revolt at Changchun in 1948; his troops became the PLA 50th Army.

李白.note: 1910–1949. Communist radio operator in Shanghai, executed on the eve of the city's liberation; not to be confused with the Tang poet. His story inspired the film The Unfailing Radio Wave.

沈崇.note: The Peking University student whose rape by U.S. Marines in December 1946 set off nationwide student protests.

五一口号.note: The Communists' May 1, 1948 slogans, whose call to convene a Political Consultative Conference and found a coalition government opened the road to the People's Republic.

罗瑞卿.note: 1906–1978. First minister of public security of the People's Republic (from 1949); ranked Senior General in 1955. Brought down in December 1965 on the eve of the Cultural Revolution.

扬帆.note: 1912–1999. Chief of the Shanghai Public Security Bureau; arrested in 1954–55 in the “Pan-Yang case” and rehabilitated in the 1980s.

彭真.note: 1902–1997. Mayor of Beijing and head of the Party's political-legal work; purged in 1966 as first of the “Peng-Luo-Lu-Yang” clique.

谢富治.note: 1909–1972. Minister of public security from 1959; a driver of the “smash the police, procuratorate, and courts” campaign, posthumously expelled from the Party in 1980.

李震.note: Minister of public security who died in 1973, officially a suicide, in a case never fully resolved.

谭甫仁.note: Chairman of the Yunnan Revolutionary Committee, assassinated in 1970.

马步芳.note: The Nationalist Muslim warlord of Qinghai.

侯宝林.note: 1917–1993. The most celebrated xiangsheng (comic-dialogue) performer of his day.

段云鹏.note: The cat-burglar (“flying thief”) recruited by Nationalist intelligence; see also Chapter 11.

杨杰.note: 1889–1949. Nationalist general and military theorist, assassinated in Hong Kong on the eve of the new Political Consultative Conference.

司徒雷登.note: American ambassador to China 1946–1949; the conventional English form is used.

公安部.note: The People's Republic's ministry of public security (police), founded in 1949 out of the Military Commission's Public Security Department.

镇反运动.note: The mass campaign of 1950–1953; see the footnote at its first appearance in this chapter.

文化大革命.note: 1966–1976. The author uses the term in quotation marks throughout, marking the settled Party verdict that it was a catastrophe.

砸烂公检法.note: The Cultural Revolution slogan against the legal apparatus; kept as a slogan and glossed.

一百单八将.note: The 108 heroes of Water Margin; the nickname for the 101 trainees plus 7 instructors of the first public-security class.
